factsAccepted: Fully-loaded CAC has risen to ~$220k (sales + marketing + sales-engineering + subsidized implementation), LTV/CAC fell from 3.4 to 1.6, and CAC payback extended from 18 to 34 months. At a 1.6 ratio and 34-month payback, the company spends far ahead of customer profitability, and the economics are below the threshold needed to be fundable.

The sales motion is expensive and slow: average sales cycle 6.5 months and sales-engineering hours per deal up 45%, while win rate is stable at 22%. The rising SE intensity inflates CAC without improving conversion, indicating the cost of acquiring each customer is structurally high, especially in the largest deals.

Implementation averages 16 weeks and is heavily subsidized: the company absorbs ~60% of implementation cost, roughly $48k per customer, which is loaded into CAC. Implementation is genuinely complex (data migration, pipeline setup, governance), so the subsidy is a structural drag on acquisition economics rather than a one-off.

~40% of churned customers leave within the first 9 months, citing implementation delays and unrealized value, which shortens realized LTV before payback (34 months) is ever reached. Gross retention is 90%. Early-life churn does not just lose revenue; it directly worsens the LTV/CAC ratio by truncating lifetime on the most expensively acquired customers.

Segmentation matters: large enterprise deals have the longest cycles and most expensive delivery (and worst LTV/CAC) but highest ACV, while mid-size deals show materially better LTV/CAC. Competitors with simpler scopes run shorter cycles and cheaper delivery, pressuring the company's cost-to-acquire-and-serve in the enterprise segment.
